title: Building with Anthropic Claude: Prompt Workshop with Zack Witten
talk_summary: Zack Witten live-debugs audience prompts in the Anthropic console, demonstrating concrete prompting mechanics: XML-tag separation, instruction ordering, assistant prefill for JSON, stop sequences, and few-shot examples. He repeatedly argues that offloading deterministic work to code beats trying to force it via prompt wording.

takeaways.technique: Assistant prefill + stop sequences for structured output
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of begging the model to 'only output JSON', they prefill the assistant turn with the opening of the desired output (e.g. '```json' or '{') so the model continues in-format, and add the closing tag to stop sequences so it hard-stops and isn't billed for trailing prose.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you're putting some words in quad's mouth as we call it and then when Claude continues from there it assumes that it's already said whatever you told it

takeaways.technique: Offload determinism to code, not prompts
takeaways.what_they_do: Repeatedly strips 'you must output JSON / don't add preamble' boilerplate from prompts and replaces it with prefill, regex extraction, and stop sequences; also recommends checking formatting in code rather than model-grading it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a lot of times it's cheaper and easier to do a little bit of work outside of a call to the llm and not even worry about prompting

takeaways.technique: Few-shot examples dominate other prompt tweaks
takeaways.what_they_do: Says most of the gain in prompt quality comes from curating a few excellent input/output examples (including contrasting good/bad pairs with reasoning), not from wording tweaks; prefers one high-quality example over many truncated ones.
takeaways.evidence_quote: most of the effort most of the gains of writing a good prompt is literally just picking the perfect document that goes here

takeaways.technique: Code-checkable evals over model-grading for format; model-grading only for squishy outputs
takeaways.what_they_do: When asked about testing prompts at scale, he insists formatting/structural checks be done in code (regex/tags), reserving LLM-as-judge or humans for subjective outputs; also warns numeric scales are poorly calibrated so cap granularity at ~5 classes.
takeaways.evidence_quote: formatting is something that I can check in code so if I can do anything in code and I don't have to call the LM

takeaways.technique: Extract quotes before summarizing to cut hallucination
takeaways.what_they_do: For summarization/hallucination-prone tasks, first have the model extract relevant verbatim quotes from the source, then summarize only from those quotes (with prefill to suppress preamble).
takeaways.evidence_quote: the best trick that I know for getting around hallucinations in a case like this is to have the model extract relevant quotes first

takeaways.what_they_do: Puts long documents/information above instructions because instructions closer to the end are followed more tightly; uses negative prompting sparingly (once, lightly) to avoid reverse-psychology fixation.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instructions are more tightly followed the closer they are to the bottom of the prompt as a rule
